newsitem.title: JAPAN: Most Japan lawmakers back constitution change - poll.
newsitem.headline: Most Japan lawmakers back constitution change - poll.

text.p: Sixty percent of Japanese parliamentarians favour amending the country's U.S.-imposed Constitution, according to a survey published by a major newspaper on Friday.

Most of the 60.4 percent of lawmakers who want the 50-year-old Constitution amended said revisions were needed to enable Japan to cope with international changes, the mass-circulation Yomiuri Shimbun said.

The Yomiuri said the part of the present Constitution which troubled parliamentarians the most was Article 9, the "peace clause" which stipulates: "The Japanese people forever renounce war as a sovereign right of the nation and the threat or use of force as means of settling international disputes."
The Constitution was drawn up under the supervision of U.S. Occupation troops at the end of World War Two.

Japan was criticised during the 1991 Gulf War when it said constitutional bans on collective security efforts allowed it to donate billions of dollars in cash but not join international forces which drove Iraq from Kuwait.

The 34.8 percent of the respondents who said they opposed revising the Constitution -- discussion of which has long been taboo because of sharp polarisation in domestic politics and Asian neighbours' memories of Japanese wartime militarism -- said Japan should be proud of the pacifist document.

The Yomiuri, a conservative daily which has long been a prominent advocate of rewriting the Constitution, polled all 752 legislators from both the upper and lower chambers of parliament and received replies from 465.

Results of the poll, conducted prior to the 50th anniversary on May 3 of the enactment of the Constitution, contrasted with separate surveys the newspaper held last year of ordinary citizens and experts, the daily said.

A March 1996 nationwide poll of citizens found 47 percent supported amending the Constitution, while a poll of academics and intellectuals last August found 57 percent in favour of revisions, it said.

Lawmakers from Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto's conservative Liberal Democratic Party and LDP splinter groups in the opposition -- the New Frontier Party, Sakigake and the Sun Party -- strongly favoured an amendment, the newspaper said.
Liberal and left-leaning parties, such as the Democratic Party, the Social Democratic Party and the Communists, were just as strongly against changes, the Yomiuri said.
Under the Constitution, an amendment requires the approval of two-thirds of the members of parliament.
